To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
multinational enterprises have an ambiguous impact on the wages in the host countries.

multinational activity can have a positive or a negative effect on host country wages depending on the capital intensity of the multinational and local sectors, and the magnitude of the knowledge spillovers to local firms.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (i) the impact of multinational activity on the host country wages; (ii) the role of capital intensity differences between multinational and local sectors in the host country; (iii) the role of knowledge spillover in explaining the wage effect of multinational activity; (iv) the role of foreign direct investment in explaining the wage effects of multinational activity.
the impact of MNE activity on wages in the home country.
the impact of multinational activity on the host country’s wages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impact of MNE activity on the host country wages is ambiguous.
MNEs may have a negative effect on the wages of unskilled workers, a positive effect on skilled workers and a positive effect on the economy’s capital stock.
the impact on wages of multinational enterprises is ambiguous and depends on a number of factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while foreign knowledge spillovers and the inflow capital from abroad tend to raise the host country wages, the effect of the transfer of capital from foreign firms to the host country is ambiguous and may even lead to a reduction in wages.

multinational enterprises can increase or decrease wages in the host economy, but the direction depends on the relative intensity of capital use in multinational and local sectors, as well as the amount of capital and technology transferred to the host economy from abroad and the extent of technology diffusion.
multinational enterprises can be a blessing or a curse for host countries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of multinational activity on wages depends crucially on how foreign knowledge spillovers are transmitted to indigenous firms.

the expansion of multinational firms in the host country may increase the wages of local workers if foreign firms have a lower capital intensity than indigenous firms and the knowledge spillover effect is sufficiently large.
the effect of multinational enterprises on host country wages is not necessarily negative and depends on the relative importance of the various mechanisms at play.
